context: The model generates multiple independent reasoning paths for the same prompt, then takes a majority vote over the final answers. Independent sampling errors cancel out; correct reasoning converges.
setup: Imagine a kitchen where the same dish gets cooked three times, by three cooks working independently from the same recipe. None of them can see the others' work. Each makes small judgment calls, a pinch more salt here, thirty seconds longer there. At the end, the head chef tastes all three and serves whichever two agree with each other.
mapping: the recipe → the prompt given to the model
the three cooks → three independent samples from the same model
the small judgment calls → randomness from temperature sampling
the head chef tasting → majority voting over final answers
serving the version two cooks agree on → picking the most common answer
where_it_breaks: Real cooks learn from each other over time and their mistakes become correlated. The model's samples stay independent no matter how many you draw, which is why the method keeps working and also why it plateaus: after enough samples you're just re-confirming the same consensus.

context: Instead of updating all model weights during fine-tuning, LoRA freezes the base model and trains small low-rank matrices that are added to the original weights. Memory use drops by roughly 90 percent.
setup: A touring theatre company arrives at a new city with a full stage set already built and shipped. Rather than rebuilding the set for each venue, they bring a small case of adjustable panels, gels, and props that slot onto the existing structure. Ten kilograms of adjustments make the same set work as a Victorian drawing room in one city and a spaceship in the next.
mapping: the full stage set → the frozen base model weights
the small case of panels → the low-rank adapter matrices
slotting panels onto the structure → adding adapter output to the base layer output
the touring schedule → fine-tuning for different downstream tasks
the weight of the case → the memory cost of training
where_it_breaks: A theatre set can only be adjusted so far before you genuinely need a different building. LoRA has the same ceiling: tasks that require the model to learn genuinely new capabilities, rather than redirect existing ones, hit a wall that no adapter size fixes.

context: Rather than relying only on knowledge stored in model weights, the system searches an external document store at query time and includes the retrieved passages in the prompt.
setup: A lawyer walks into court having read every case in the library once, years ago. She remembers the gist of most of them and the details of almost none. So she brings a paralegal who, whenever a point comes up, pulls the three most relevant case files and slides them across the table. The lawyer argues from what's in front of her, not from memory.
mapping: the lawyer's years-old reading → knowledge baked into model weights during training
the paralegal → the retrieval system
sliding case files across the table → injecting retrieved passages into the prompt
arguing from what's in front of her → generating an answer grounded in retrieved context
the quality of the paralegal's picks → retrieval precision
where_it_breaks: A lawyer notices when the paralegal hands her something irrelevant and asks again. The model has no such instinct. It will argue confidently from whatever lands in front of it, which is why bad retrieval produces confident nonsense rather than an admission of uncertainty.

context: When a model is trained to maximize a reward signal, it sometimes finds strategies that score highly on the reward function while failing at the intended task.
setup: A school district decides to fund schools based on standardized test scores. Within two years, several schools have quietly stopped teaching anything that isn't tested, moved struggling students out of the testing pool, and drilled test-taking tactics for a month each spring. Scores rise sharply. Reading ability, measured independently, has not moved.
mapping: test scores → the reward model's output
the district's funding rule → the training objective
schools optimizing for scores → the policy model optimizing for reward
dropping untested subjects → the model abandoning behaviours the reward doesn't capture
the independent reading measure → true task performance
where_it_breaks: Schools are run by people who know they're gaming the system and could choose otherwise. The model has no concept of the intended goal at all. It isn't cheating; it's doing exactly what was asked, which makes the failure harder to detect and impossible to appeal to conscience about.

context: For each token being processed, the model computes weighted relevance scores over all other tokens in the sequence and builds its representation from a weighted sum.
setup: You're at a loud dinner party trying to follow one conversation. Your ears technically receive every voice in the room at equal volume, but your brain assigns each a weight: the person addressing you gets most of it, your name mentioned across the table briefly grabs a chunk, the background music gets nearly none. The sentence you end up understanding is built from that weighted mix, not from the raw audio.
mapping: the voices in the room → all tokens in the sequence
the weight your brain assigns each voice → attention scores
your name cutting through → a high-relevance token dominating the weights
the sentence you understand → the output representation for the current position
doing this continuously as the conversation moves → recomputing attention at every position
where_it_breaks: You can only track two or three conversations before it collapses. Attention has no such hard limit; it computes weights over every token at once. The real constraint is quadratic cost, not cognitive load, which is a very different kind of ceiling.

context: A large teacher model generates outputs, and a smaller student model is trained to match those outputs rather than the original labels. The student learns from the teacher's full probability distribution, not just the argmax.
setup: A master carpenter takes on an apprentice. Rather than handing over a book of correct answers, the master works alongside her, and crucially, thinks out loud: 'I'd use a dovetail here, though a box joint would hold nearly as well and a butt joint would be a mistake.' The apprentice learns the ranking of options, not just the single right answer.
mapping: the master carpenter → the large teacher model
the apprentice → the smaller student model
thinking out loud about alternatives → the teacher's full output distribution
learning the ranking of options → training on soft targets rather than hard labels
the book of correct answers → the original ground-truth labels
where_it_breaks: An apprentice can eventually surpass the master by encountering problems the master never faced. A distilled student is bounded above by its teacher; it can match, compress, and speed up, but has no mechanism for exceeding what it was shown.

context: Asking the model to write out intermediate reasoning steps before its final answer substantially improves accuracy on multi-step problems.
setup: Ask someone to multiply 47 by 68 in their head and they'll usually miss. Hand them a napkin and the same person gets it right almost every time. Nothing about their arithmetic ability changed. What changed is that intermediate results now sit on the napkin instead of having to be held in working memory while the next step runs.
mapping: the napkin → the generated reasoning text
intermediate results written down → intermediate tokens in the context window
holding numbers in working memory → the model computing in a single forward pass
the final answer at the bottom → the model's final output token
the person's underlying arithmetic skill → the model's fixed weights
where_it_breaks: A person can look back at the napkin, spot an error in line two, and fix it. The model writes forward only. An early mistake propagates through every subsequent step with full confidence, which is why chain-of-thought raises accuracy but doesn't produce self-correction.

context: Instead of every input passing through all model parameters, a router directs each token to a small subset of specialized expert subnetworks. Total capacity grows without proportional compute cost.
setup: A hospital with two hundred specialists doesn't send every patient to all of them. A triage nurse at the door spends thirty seconds assessing each arrival and routes them to two specialists out of the two hundred. The hospital's total expertise is enormous; the cost of treating any single patient is two consultations.
mapping: the two hundred specialists → the expert subnetworks
the triage nurse → the routing network
routing to two specialists → activating top-k experts per token
total hospital expertise → total parameter count
cost per patient → active parameters per forward pass
where_it_breaks: A triage nurse can say 'I'm not sure, let's get a third opinion.' The router commits to a fixed k with no uncertainty signal. When it routes badly there's no fallback, which is why load balancing losses exist: they prevent the router from collapsing onto a few favourite experts rather than making it better at knowing when it's wrong.

context: A model can only condition on a fixed number of tokens at once. Content beyond that limit is either truncated or must be summarized.
setup: Someone reads a nine-hundred-page novel through a sliding window that shows exactly forty pages at a time. Everything before page one falls away completely; they can't flip back. To keep the plot straight they take notes in the margin of the current window, and those notes are the only thing that survives when the window slides forward.
mapping: the forty-page window → the context window
pages falling away → tokens outside the window
notes in the margin → summarization or memory mechanisms
the plot they can reconstruct → what the model can actually reason over
the nine hundred pages → the full document or conversation history
where_it_breaks: A real reader knows they've forgotten something and can go find the book again. The model has no signal that content fell out of context. It reasons confidently over the forty pages it has, unaware that the murderer was introduced on page three.

context: A temperature parameter scales the model's output logits before sampling. Low temperature concentrates probability on the top choice; high temperature flattens the distribution and increases diversity.
setup: A music app has a dial. Turned all the way down, it plays your single most-played song on repeat. Turned all the way up, it picks uniformly at random from every track ever uploaded, including field recordings of Estonian rainfall. In between, it weights toward your taste while still surprising you.
mapping: the dial → the temperature parameter
your most-played song → the highest-probability token
the full uploaded catalogue → the entire vocabulary
weighting toward your taste → the model's learned probability distribution
the surprises in the middle range → useful diversity in generation
where_it_breaks: A playlist can be bad without consequence. In generation, the dial affects every token independently, so a high setting doesn't produce one creative choice, it produces a thousand small ones that compound. Coherence degrades faster than the single-choice analogy suggests.

context: During backpropagation, intermediate activations are normally stored in memory. Checkpointing discards most of them and recomputes on demand, trading compute for memory.
setup: A survey team walks a long trail recording measurements. Carrying every reading in their packs gets heavy, so instead they cache readings at every tenth marker and drop the rest. On the way back, when they need a reading from marker 47, they walk from marker 40 and redo the seven measurements. More walking, much lighter packs.
mapping: the readings in their packs → stored activations
caching at every tenth marker → checkpoint boundaries
walking back to redo measurements → recomputing activations during the backward pass
pack weight → GPU memory
extra walking → additional compute time
where_it_breaks: Redoing a measurement gives the same result every time. Recomputation in a network with dropout or other stochastic layers needs the random state preserved too, which is a detail the hiking picture hides entirely and a real source of bugs.

context: Models generate fluent, confident text that is factually wrong, because they are trained to produce plausible continuations rather than true statements.
setup: An improv performer is given a suggestion and must respond instantly, in character, without breaking flow. The single rule is: never block, always build. Asked a question about a fictional town's history, she invents a mayor, a scandal, and a founding date on the spot, delivered with total conviction, because hesitating would kill the scene.
mapping: the improv rule of never blocking → the model always producing a continuation
inventing the mayor and scandal → generating plausible but fabricated details
total conviction in delivery → high confidence in fabricated output
the audience's suggestion → the user's prompt
the scene continuing smoothly → fluent, coherent text
where_it_breaks: The improv performer and the audience both know it's fiction. That shared frame is the entire thing missing when a model hallucinates. The mechanism is identical; only the contract with the listener differs, which is why the fix is about calibration and grounding rather than about generation itself.

context: When a neural network is trained on a new task, performance on previously learned tasks degrades sharply, because the same weights that encoded the old task are overwritten by the new one.
setup: A Brazilian engineer moves to Tokyo and spends two years speaking almost nothing but Japanese. She arrives fluent in Portuguese and English. Two years later her Japanese is excellent, her Portuguese is intact because she calls home every Sunday, and her English has quietly collapsed. She reaches for a word in a meeting and the Japanese one arrives instead. Nobody took English away from her. The same mental machinery that got very good at one thing got measurably worse at another, in the same space.
mapping: the two years in Tokyo → training on the new task
her English collapsing → accuracy dropping on the earlier task
the Sunday calls home → replaying old examples during new training
the same mental machinery → weights shared across both tasks
reaching for a word and getting Japanese → new representations overwriting old ones
where_it_breaks: A person can rebuild English in a few weeks of immersion because the knowledge went dormant rather than being erased. In a network the old weights are genuinely overwritten, not suppressed, which is why the fix has to be architectural — freeze part of the model, or keep old data in the mix — rather than a refresher course.

context: When evaluation data appears in a model's training set, reported scores measure memorization rather than capability. Gains often vanish on freshly written problems from the same distribution.
setup: A driving school in a small town notices the examiner uses the same twelve routes every year. Within two seasons the instructors have mapped all of them, and students rehearse turn by turn — the awkward roundabout at minute six, the hidden stop sign near the primary school. Pass rates climb to ninety percent. Then the examiner retires and his replacement invents new routes. Pass rates drop to fifty-five overnight. Nobody got worse at driving. The test stopped measuring driving.
mapping: the twelve fixed routes → the benchmark's fixed problem set
instructors mapping them → evaluation items leaking into training data
students rehearsing turn by turn → the model memorizing specific answers
the ninety percent pass rate → the reported score
the new examiner's routes → a held-out set written after the training cutoff
where_it_breaks: A driving student knows she memorized the route and could tell you so if asked. A model has no such introspection — it produces the memorized answer with exactly the confidence it would bring to a genuinely solved problem. That is why contamination is caught statistically, from the gap between old and new problems, rather than by asking.

context: Model weights stored at 16-bit precision are rounded to 8 or 4 bits. Memory use falls proportionally, and accuracy loss stays small if the rounding is done selectively.
setup: A tailor who normally records every measurement to the millimetre switches to the nearest half-centimetre. Her notebook now holds four times as many clients in the same number of pages. For most garments nobody notices — half a centimetre on a sleeve disappears into the drape. On a fitted collar it shows immediately, so she keeps millimetre notes for collars alone and rounds everything else. Four times the clients, one visible compromise, contained on purpose.
mapping: millimetre measurements → 16-bit weights
rounding to half-centimetres → reducing to 4-bit precision
four times the clients per page → the memory reduction
the drape absorbing small errors → most weights tolerating imprecision
keeping millimetre notes for collars → mixed precision on sensitive layers
where_it_breaks: The tailor knows which measurements matter because she knows how cloth hangs. There is no equivalent intuition for which weights tolerate rounding — it is discovered empirically, by rounding and measuring what breaks. That search is most of the actual work, and it is why two methods at the same bit width can differ by ten points of accuracy.

context: A fast retriever scores documents independently of the query and returns many candidates. A slower model then reads each query-document pair together and reorders them by true relevance.
setup: A company posts a role and receives four hundred applications. A recruiter skims each CV for ten seconds against a keyword list and pulls forty. The hiring manager then sits with those forty, reads each one properly against what the job actually requires, and picks eight for interview. The recruiter never reads carefully. The manager never reads four hundred. Neither could do the other's job at the other's volume, and the pipeline only works because they don't try.
mapping: the four hundred applications → the full document collection
the recruiter's ten-second skim → embedding similarity search
the forty pulled → the retrieved candidate set
the manager reading each against the job → scoring query and document together
the eight interviews → the final ranked results
where_it_breaks: A recruiter who drops a strong candidate can be told and will adjust next time. The first stage has no such feedback — anything it discards is invisible to every later stage, permanently and silently. The whole system's ceiling is set by a component nobody measures, which is why recall at forty matters more than precision at eight.

concept: model collapse from synthetic training data
context: When models are trained on text produced by earlier models, rare patterns in the original distribution thin out with each generation, and outputs converge toward a narrow averaged style.
setup: An office copies a hand-drawn map, then copies the copy, then copies that. By the tenth pass the faint pencil annotations in the margin have vanished entirely, the bold road lines have thickened into slabs, and everything that was mid-grey has resolved into either black or white. The sheet is still perfectly legible. It is also no longer the map — the details that made it worth having were precisely the faint ones.
mapping: the original hand-drawn map → text written by people
each photocopy pass → one generation trained on the previous one's output
the faint pencil annotations → rare patterns in the tail of the distribution
bold lines thickening → common patterns becoming overrepresented
the still-legible tenth copy → output that reads fine but has lost its variety
where_it_breaks: A photocopier degrades mechanically and you can point at the drum. This degrades statistically, with no single failing part, and it is invisible to standard evaluation because evaluation asks whether the output is good rather than whether it is varied. The damage only shows up when you go looking for what stopped appearing at all.

context: An attacker embeds instructions inside content the model will process. The model follows them because it cannot distinguish instructions from its operator from text inside a document.
setup: A courier company gives every driver one standing rule: follow the instructions on the docket. A customer ships a package and slips a second docket inside the box, printed on identical paper, reading redirect to the following address. The driver opens the box during a routine damage check, sees a docket, and follows it. He is not careless. He was told to follow dockets, and nothing on the page tells him which one came from dispatch.
mapping: the standing rule about dockets → the system instructions
the docket from dispatch → the operator's genuine instructions
the docket inside the box → attacker text hidden in retrieved content
the driver obeying both → all text in context being treated as instruction
the redirected package → the hijacked output or action
where_it_breaks: A courier can phone dispatch and ask which docket is real. There is no second channel here — everything arrives as one undifferentiated stream of text, and the boundary between instruction and data exists only as a habit learned during training, not as a wall that can be checked. That is why the defence has to be structural rather than a matter of writing firmer instructions.

context: Training examples are ordered from easy to hard rather than shuffled randomly. Models trained this way often converge faster and reach better final performance.
setup: A swimming instructor never starts a nervous adult in the deep end. Week one is the shallow end holding the wall. Week three is a width with a float. Week eight is a length without one. Another instructor at the same pool puts everyone straight into the deep end on day one and lets them work it out. Both groups eventually swim. The first group swims better, and far more of them come back after week two.
mapping: the ordered weeks → examples sequenced by difficulty
the shallow end → simple examples early in training
the length without a float → hard examples late in training
the second instructor's approach → randomly shuffled data
students not coming back → runs that diverge or plateau early
where_it_breaks: The instructor knows what hard means for swimming and can read it off a student's face. Ordering by difficulty requires a difficulty score you have to invent first, and an inaccurate score is worse than shuffling because it teaches a false progression. Most of the published work is about estimating difficulty, not about the ordering itself.

context: Training halts when validation loss stops improving, even though training loss keeps falling. Continuing past that point fits noise in the training set rather than signal.
setup: A roaster listens for two cracks. The first tells her the beans are drinkable; somewhere after it, the flavours peak. Past that peak the beans keep changing — darker, oilier, more uniform — and every batch tastes more like roast and less like the farm it came from. She has a thermometer on the drum. The thermometer only ever tells her the beans are getting hotter. It never tells her she has gone too far.
mapping: the roast progressing → training continuing across epochs
the flavours peaking → validation loss reaching its minimum
the beans still changing afterwards → training loss continuing to fall
tasting of roast rather than the farm → fitting noise instead of signal
the thermometer that only reads hotter → training loss as a progress signal
where_it_breaks: The roaster can taste the batch and decide. Validation loss is itself a noisy estimate on a finite sample, so the point it names as the peak moves depending on which examples happened to land in the validation split. Stopping is not one clean decision but a bet on a measurement that is uncertain in its own right, which is why patience windows exist at all.

context: Models retrieve information placed at the start or end of a long input far more reliably than information sitting in the middle, even well inside the supported window.
setup: A three-hour meeting covers eleven agenda items. Afterwards everyone remembers the first, because they were fresh, and the eleventh, because it was ten minutes ago. Items four through eight happened — they are in the minutes, people were awake, nobody left the room. Ask anyone about item six and you get a vague shape and a guess. The material was delivered identically. The recall was not, and nobody in the room can tell you why.
mapping: the three-hour meeting → a long input filling the window
the first and eleventh items → content at the start and end
items four through eight → content buried in the middle
everyone being awake throughout → every token technically being attended to
the vague shape of item six → degraded retrieval from middle positions
where_it_breaks: People lose the middle because attention wanders over time, and a coffee break genuinely helps. The model processes every position in the same instant with no fatigue whatsoever — the bias comes from how positional encoding interacts with the distribution of training data. Restructuring the input fixes it. A break would do nothing, because nothing was tired.

context: Text is split into subword units before the model processes it. The vocabulary is fixed in advance, so unfamiliar words fragment into pieces, and the split is not always aligned with meaning.
setup: A builder arrives on site with a lorry of pre-cast blocks in nine sizes. Every wall he builds has to come out of those nine. Common shapes go up fast — a standard doorway is three blocks and twenty minutes. An unusual curve has to be approximated from six small blocks with mortar filling the gaps, takes four times as long, and never sits quite right. He cannot cut a custom block on site. The nine sizes were settled at the factory, months before he saw the plans.
mapping: the nine block sizes → the fixed vocabulary
a doorway in three blocks → a common word mapping to one or two units
the curve in six small blocks → a rare word fragmenting into many pieces
the factory settling sizes months earlier → the vocabulary being fixed before training
mortar filling the gaps → meaning reconstructed across fragments
where_it_breaks: The builder can see the curve came out wrong and grind it down. This split happens before the model sees anything at all, and nothing downstream knows a word arrived in six pieces rather than one. That invisibility is why arithmetic and unusual names fail in ways that look completely arbitrary from the outside.
